qs.q: A 19-year-old university student is diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis after presenting with fever, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and abnormal liver function tests. What specific activity restriction should be strongly advised?
o: Avoid contact sports for six to eight weeks
Isolation from peers for fourteen days
Complete dietary restriction of dairy products
Strict bed rest for at least six months
qs.e: Due to the risk of splenic enlargement and subsequent rupture in infectious mononucleosis, patients must avoid contact sports for 6 to 8 weeks. Bed rest for six months is excessively restrictive and unnecessary.

qs.q: Streptococcal tonsillitis requires prompt recognition and treatment because it can lead to all of the following complications EXCEPT
qs.e: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus rather than a streptococcal bacterial infection. The three classic complications of untreated streptococcal tonsillitis include quinsy, glomerulonephritis, and rheumatic fever.

qs.q: Streptococcal tonsillitis is important to recognize early because it can lead to all EXCEPT
qs.e: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by EBV, not streptococcal infection. The three important complications of streptococcal tonsillitis are quinsy, glomerulonephritis, and rheumatic fever.

qs.q: Streptococcal tonsillitis must be identified and treated early to prevent
o: Epiglottitis, croup, and spread to the retropharyngeal space
Peritonsillar abscess, acute rheumatic fever, and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
Viral superinfection, mastoiditis, and descending necrotising mediastinitis
Diphtheria pseudomembrane, myocarditis, and peripheral neuropathy from exotoxin
qs.e: Untreated group A streptococcal tonsillitis risks peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), acute rheumatic fever, and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — all potentially serious non-suppurative complications.
